Triggers.value: Someone getting emotionally close to me

Maladaptive Strategies.value: Paying attention to or looking at my own body
Allowing myself to feel any strong emotion

Threat.value: My body feels constantly tense and ready to react to danger
I listen for sounds that might mean someone is entering my home
I feel on guard even inside my own home

Memory.value: When memories come to mind of what happened, I feel my body is in the same position as when the frightening event occurred.
I remember the frightening event as a few moments, and each moment is a picture in my mind.
When I remember the event I feel intense shame

Negative Appraisals.value: I am no longer capable of doing the things that defined me
I have lost my faith in people, life, or a higher power

issues.item: Triggers: Auditory (Explosion): Explosion or bang sounds
issues.explanation: 'Explosion or bang sounds' is hard to reconcile with the trauma type of chronic physical abuse by a romantic partner unless there is additional history not represented elsewhere. The rest of the profile centers on interpersonal/home-based threat, emotional closeness, family comments, shame, weakness, and hypervigilance for someone entering the home. An explosion-specific trigger pulls toward a very different trauma context and is not supported by the memory, threat, or appraisal items.

issues.item: Maladaptive Strategies: Self-Harm Distraction: I hurt myself physically to stop thinking about the event
issues.explanation: Self-harm as a distraction strategy is not impossible, but in this profile it is weakly supported by the rest of the selected items. The maladaptive strategy set otherwise reflects avoidance and conflict-generation, while the connected nodes emphasize home intrusion vigilance, bodily reenactment, shame, weakness, and loss of trust. Because Maladaptive Strategies is strongly linked to Triggers and somewhat to Threat/Negative Appraisals here, a severe self-injurious coping item stands out as insufficiently integrated with the rest of the formulation and item pattern.

issues.item: Seeking Conflict: I pick arguments or create drama to distract myself from the trauma
issues.explanation: 'Seeking Conflict' is hard to reconcile with the rest of this profile. The patient's trauma is intimate partner physical abuse, and the other nodes describe hypervigilance, shame, weakness, loss of trust, and avoidance. Deliberately creating interpersonal conflict is a marked shift in style that is not supported by the accompanying threat, memory, appraisal, or trigger items, making this maladaptive strategy clinically incoherent in this profile.

vignette: Elena remembered the afternoon the violence finally erupted, how it had begun not with a shouted warning but with a slow, chilling withdrawal that made her reach for her husband’s arm, only to have him shrug her off with a force that sent her stumbling into the wall. When he finally swung his fist, the kitchen door had burst open behind him, the loud slam echoing through the rafters as his voice rose and his hands closed around her shoulders with bruising certainty. Years later, the specific weight of that betrayal had calcified into a hypervigilant wiring; any comment from her adult children about family harmony now felt like a precursor to conflict, any moment when someone tried to sit close to her on the sofa triggered a sudden recoil, and the sharp click of a latch or the heavy thud of a closing door instantly pulled her attention outward. The moment a family member made a sweeping remark about reconciliation, Elena’s physiology would instantly shift into a state of constant readiness; her shoulders would hike and her chest would tighten, her body feeling constantly tense and ready to react to danger, while her mind would simultaneously flip open to the vivid, fragmented snapshots of the kitchen that flashed behind her eyes. Each auditory trigger, like the sudden snap of a gate or the heavy sigh of a closing door, did not just spark a startle response; it pulled the same paralyzing bodily reenactment forward, forcing her to feel her body as if it were trapped in the exact, defenseless position from years ago, and the sudden shame on recall that followed would immediately poison her outlook, convincing her that she was no longer capable of trust and that she had been a weak person to allow the abuse to continue so long. Once those judgments about her own worthlessness and shattered faith took root, they dictated her daily retreat over the following months; Elena began systematically avoiding her own body by constantly checking mirrors with clinical detachment rather than acceptance, forbidding herself from allowing herself to feel any strong emotion by keeping her voice flat and her schedule rigid, and actively avoiding people by canceling pharmacy shifts and turning down social calls, convinced that isolation was the only safe harbor. Yet this internalized belief that she was fundamentally broken and had lost faith in people did not shield her; instead, it constantly fed her memories, causing the shame on recall to return whenever she tried to rest, and it actively amplified her triggers, making a simple knock on her front door feel as menacing as a violent intrusion because her mind was already primed to interpret neutrality as a prelude to harm. When the fragmented pictures of the assault held her attention, the physiological alarm would inevitably flare; her lungs would constrict as her body on alert system misread the quiet of her living room as a prelude to attack, and she would find herself standing near the entryway, intrusion monitoring her surroundings with narrowed eyes. This recurrent imagery also sharpened her sensitivity to the outside world, so that a car backfiring or a neighbor’s heavy boot on the pavement would instantly become a new trigger, dragging her attention away from her work and toward the hallway because her mind could no longer distinguish between the past violence and the present environment. Elena’s chronic state of alert at home and her relentless intrusion monitoring demanded a toll; to manage the exhausting weight of her body on alert, she deepened her avoidance of feelings and withdrawal from others, knowing that staying numb was the only way to stop the constant shaking. The relentless tension also warped her recollection, making the snapshot memories bleed into one another until the bodily reenactment felt like a continuous present, and it hardened her negative appraisals, reinforcing the belief that she had lost faith in life and that she was simply no longer capable of recovery. Even her baseline vigilance looped back to sharpen her sensitivity, so that any sudden shift in her household’s rhythm—her husband’s lighter on the counter, a phone ringing—became a fresh trigger, demanding immediate attention. Her retreat only deepened the very convictions she hoped to escape; by consistently avoiding people and refusing to engage with her own physical sensations, Elena convinced herself further that she was a weak person and that her past was a permanent marker of failure, which in turn made her even more hyper-aware of ordinary sounds and comments, interpreting them through the lens of her own perceived deficiency. At seventy-four, working the dispensary counter, she finally sat in Dr. Aris’s office because a customer’s heavy sigh as the door shut behind him made her body feel constantly tense and ready to react to danger, and her avoidance of people had turned every prescription handoff into a source of dread. What she most hoped for was not a return to who she used to be, but simply a quiet mind that would stop bracing for the next blow.
